name: Diego Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no links to your employer, AI firms, unions or government. This is confidential. What does a usual shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an excavator at East Ridge mine, loading broken rock into the haul trucks. After my vocational course, it took years to get the bucket smooth enough that drivers stopped complaining. My partner works at a local school, and we have two children and a mortgage. I use an AI app now and then to tidy notes, but I trust my own eyes at the face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a little help with logs is fine if the machines leave our shifts alone. The app can make my handover note readable, which my mate jokes is a miracle. I would still check the bucket and the rock myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the mine would keep needing experienced operators. Our savings cover more than half a year, and another mine is recruiting across town. I would worry more about ordinary breakdowns than an AI sales pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would carry on loading trucks and use the note app when my handwriting is a mess. In the first year, I would compare my logged hours with payroll once a month. I would keep the normal mortgage payment and our savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. The job and household money feel steady, though a broken excavator can still spoil a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the app miss in a handover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A scrape on the bucket tooth looks small in a tidy note. I have to say where it is and show the next operator. The AI note app cannot climb down and point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check payroll if you feel secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have seen overtime entered late. Checking is a habit, not a prediction that we will lose hours. My partner checks the school payslip too.

say: A little **AI help** with handover notes is useful while operators still inspect the excavator.
I would keep the **same shifts** and check the bucket myself.
think: My **operator job** looks steady, and another mine nearby has been recruiting.
Our **savings** cover more than six months, leaving room for ordinary repairs and surprises.
do: **Keep** loading trucks on the usual East Ridge shifts.
**Use** the note app for handovers and compare logged hours with payroll monthly.
S0.quote: The AI note app cannot climb down and point.
fieldNote: He already uses an **AI app** occasionally, but treats the excavator inspection as his own responsibility.
His **savings** and nearby vacancies support a calm mood in this mild picture.

steps.text: Keep loading trucks on regular East Ridge excavator shifts
Use AI note app for excavator handovers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office will change first: buying, scheduling and handover notes. Drivers and excavator operators should see how any new schedule is made. I would ask for a trial with operators at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my bucket work lasts longer than the office paperwork, but the mine may ask us to load more trucks per hour. My partner’s school could also lose clerical hours, though I do not know. We can handle some change, yet I would watch both payslips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would volunteer to test the new shift board for one month, if operators can flag unsafe timings. I would learn the tablet screens from one of the younger drivers and keep a record of missed breaks. I would take that record to our union steward if the targets got unreasonable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I like improving a schedule, but I do not like a computer setting a pace without seeing the rock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you call a timing unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a load target leaves no time to clear a jammed bucket, I would flag it. One smooth hour does not prove every hour will be smooth. The union steward would need examples, not just my temper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner after the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the two payslips and the break log at our kitchen table. If the school hours also changed, we would revise the mortgage budget. I would not guess before seeing it.

say: I would let operators **test** any new schedule and flag unsafe load timings.
I would keep a **break log** so the union has examples if targets tighten.
think: My **bucket work** may last while office buying and scheduling change quickly.
Both household **payslips** could change if my partner’s school also cuts clerical hours.
do: **Trial** the shift board with operators for one month.
**Learn** its tablet screens from a younger driver and log missed breaks.
**Bring** unsafe targets to the union steward with examples.
feel: **Uneasy** about faster targets and possible household hour changes.
S1.quote: One smooth hour does not prove every hour will be smooth.
fieldNote: He sees **desk work** changing before excavator operation, while recognising tighter production targets could reach him.
His **trial plan** shows openness to proven tools and a union route for safety concerns.
He mentions his partner’s hours as a **possibility**, not an established school cut.

steps.text: Learn new shift board tablet screens from a driver
Bring missed break log to union steward if targets tighten

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028 changes planning first, and capable robot excavators are a separate worry around 2031. We need the union and mine to make a transition agreement before then. I would still demand safe testing in the pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine bought robot excavators when they became capable, I could lose a good wage around 2031. Our savings buy time, and other mines are nearby, but they could make the same choice. My partner’s school pay helps with the mortgage, though I cannot assume that job is untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would freeze our plan to replace the car and make an appointment with the mortgage lender this month. I would enrol in paid training on remote machine checks if the mine posted real openings. After 2028 I would keep operating the excavator, while watching whether the mine actually orders robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can make a budget and ask questions, but three years between full thinking AI and capable robots feels short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the lender appointment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how our payments change if one income falls for six months. I would not refinance without seeing the figures. We have savings, but I want to know the cost of using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a remote checks course straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there is paid time and the job has real openings. I have used tablets, but I need a real position at the end. A certificate with no position at the end is just an expensive folder. I would ask our union steward to check the offer.

say: I would tell the crew **2028** changes planning first; capable robot excavators are a separate risk around 2031.
I would ask the **union** for a transition agreement and safe robot testing.
think: My **wage** could fall around 2031 if the mine buys capable robot excavators.
Other mines might make the **same choice**, so nearby vacancies may offer only temporary shelter.
do: **Delay** replacing the family car and ask the lender about a six-month income drop.
**Enrol** in paid training for remote machine checks if the mine posts real openings.
**Keep** operating after 2028 unless the mine actually changes its equipment.
feel: **Anxious**, with a budget to examine but no guarantee of another post.
S2.quote: A certificate with no position at the end is just an expensive folder.
fieldNote: He dates the **thinking change** in 2028 and the possible hands-on threat around 2031.
His **training interest** depends on paid time and actual vacancies, which he would verify.
Savings and nearby mines provide options, but he does not assume **school income** is secure.

steps.text: Delay replacing family car during the first year
Enrol in paid remote checks training if real jobs are posted
Keep operating excavator after planning software changes in 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that five years to thinking AI and about eight to capable robots gives us room to negotiate. Operators should be in the room when the mine tests equipment. We should set a training timetable now, while the excavators still need us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight in 2031, I might still operate until robots become capable around 2034. I could learn to inspect and supervise remote equipment, if there are real jobs in that work. I would feel less rushed than in the fast picture, but I would not stake the mortgage on a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the maintenance foreman to let me spend one day a month checking excavator faults. I would take a paid remote operations course if the mine posted actual positions. We would put the car replacement on hold and make extra mortgage payments only after checking the loan terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. Eight years to possible robot work is enough to try a path and change it if the openings never come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on those maintenance days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the sensor faults that stop an excavator and how the crew verifies a repair. My bucket experience helps spot a bad reading. I would not claim to be a mechanic after one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no remote positions are posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask nearby mines about their inspection crews. If they had openings, I would apply, but I would keep my present wage until I had an offer. A mortgage means I keep my present wage until I have another offer.

say: I would use the **longer runway** to negotiate training and include operators in equipment tests.
I would set a **timetable** while current excavators still need people.
think: Inspection or remote work might be possible if **real openings** appear.
I cannot risk the **mortgage** on an unposted future job.
do: **Shadow** excavator fault checks one day each month.
**Take** a paid remote operations course if the mine posts actual positions.
**Check** loan terms before making extra mortgage payments.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadier with time to test a new route.
S3.quote: A mortgage means I keep my present wage until I have another offer.
fieldNote: He treats the later **robot date** as time to test a career path, not a guarantee of continued employment.
The move into **inspection** is conditional on real posts and paid training.
He would keep his current wage until he held another **offer**.

steps.text: Shadow excavator fault checks one day monthly
Make extra mortgage payments after checking loan terms
Apply to nearby inspection crews if mine posts no positions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the mine has a decade before thinking AI and roughly thirteen years before capable robot excavators. That is enough time to plan apprenticeships and safety tests with the crew. I would put that proposal through the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be fifty-three in 2036 and around fifty-six when capable robots arrive in 2039. Our mortgage might be nearly paid by then if we stay on schedule. I could choose between inspection work and retirement after seeing the pension figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep operating and ask to join the mine’s safety trial for new controls this year. I would keep the existing mortgage payment, ask for a pension statement, and discuss the numbers with my partner. I would help the union draft a training plan for younger operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm for my own income, though I would be uneasy about young drivers with less saved. A long warning gives me options that the two-year picture does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would want the pension statement and mortgage balance first. My partner has work too, but school hours can change. I would decide with actual numbers nearer the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would younger operators need from the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young operators need paid training places before the first robot order, with time off shifts to attend. They should not have to gamble their rent on a certificate. I would argue for that at the union meeting.

say: I would plan **apprenticeships** and safety trials before capable robots might arrive around 2039.
I would bring a **training proposal** to the union for younger workers.
think: My **mortgage** could be smaller by 2039 if payments stay on track.
I could weigh **inspection** against retirement after seeing pension figures.
do: **Join** a safety trial for new excavator controls if the mine offers one this year.
**Request** a pension statement and review it with my partner.
**Help** the union draft paid training places for younger operators.
feel: **Calm** about his own options, with concern for younger colleagues.
S4.quote: Young operators need paid training places before the first robot order, with time off shifts to attend.
fieldNote: At a possible **2039** robot date, his age and cushion give him more choices.
He wants **pension figures** before naming retirement as a decision.
His union priority shifts toward younger operators with **rent** and less savings.

steps.text: Help union draft paid training plan for younger operators
Request pension statement before deciding retirement timing

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a robot excavator could be capable around 2031, while our mortgage is still large. Paid training with posted jobs would help, along with a union agreement on safe testing. I would want the mine to show the actual timetable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask who checks a machine when the sensor says all clear and an operator sees loose rock. I would like better tools, but I want a person able to stop a dangerous load. That matters even if my own seat goes.

headlineQuote: I would like better tools, but I want a person able to stop a dangerous load.
portrait: Diego Quinn is a **43-year-old** excavator operator at East Ridge mine with a partner, two schoolchildren, a mortgage and substantial savings.
He uses an **AI note app** occasionally and will try new controls when operators can test them for safety.
In Steady Disruption he watches **targets and breaks**; faster AGI makes robot excavators around 2031 a serious income risk.
More warning lets him explore **remote checks**, inspect faults and weigh a pension decision after seeing real figures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because capable robot excavators could arrive around 2031 while his mortgage is still large.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** tied to posted jobs and a union agreement on safe testing would let him plan around any lost excavator post.
